lesson.menu_title: The Day I Decided to Leave
lesson.menu_desc: The long background and the one short morning that ended it -- past simple against past continuous, told as a story
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 6 -- The Day I Decided to Leave
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Ana Claudia Veraldi | Lesson 6 -- The Day I Decided to Leave

listenings.text: I had a very ordinary job in London and a very ordinary apartment, and for about four years I told everybody I was perfectly happy. Then one Tuesday in February I was standing on the platform at half past six, in the rain, and the train was cancelled for the third time that week. I was not angry. That is the part nobody believes. I was completely calm, and I heard myself say out loud, I am not doing this again. Two women turned and looked at me. I went home, I told my wife, and she said she had waited eleven years for me to say it. We spent that spring mulling it over, and in September we packed up the apartment. People still ask me what the last straw was. It was not the train. The train was simply the morning I finally heard myself.

The first time I wanted to leave Frankfurt I was twenty-nine, and two people talked me out of it in one single afternoon. They were being kind. They said I was restless, that everybody feels like that at twenty-nine, and that in a year I would laugh about it. They were wrong, but I believed them, and I stayed for nine more years. The second time I did not ask anybody. I was driving home on a Friday, the traffic was not moving, and I was listening to the same radio show I had listened to every Friday for nine years. I did not snap. I simply understood something. On Monday I started looking at houses, and I did not tell one single person until the contract was signed. It was not a whim. It was nine years of thinking and one Friday of deciding.

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: To suddenly lose patience after putting up with something for years
Frightening because it is large or difficult
To finally do the big thing you kept postponing
The moment when a situation changes direction for good
The final small problem that makes you finally act
Never stopping and never getting any easier

vocab.text: Notice that half of these words are about TIME, not about feeling: a turning point, the last straw, to take the plunge. A story of a decision is a story about when, and English has a word for every stage of it.

reading.rtitle: The Long Background and the Short Interruption
paras: People tell the story of leaving a city as if it were one decision made on one morning. It almost never is. Ask anybody who has moved away from a large city and the story has the same shape: a long, quiet background in which nothing seems to change, and then one very short event that changes everything.

The background is made of ordinary things. You are spending two hours a day in traffic. You are paying too much for too little space. You are sleeping badly and telling everybody that you are fine. Not one of these is a reason to leave. Together, over years, they are the reason.

Then comes the interruption. The bus does not arrive. A neighbor you have never spoken to shouts at you about a parking space. You are standing in a supermarket line at ten at night and you suddenly cannot remember why. In English we tell this part in the simple past, one short verb after another, because it happened once and it was over.

That is why the two tenses do different jobs inside the same story. The long background takes was and were plus -ing; the sharp event takes the plain past. Get them the wrong way round and the story still makes sense, but it loses its shape: everything sounds equally important, and the listener never hears the moment the decision was made.

reading.prompt: Read once, quickly. Which title fits the whole text best?
choices: How to plan a move to the countryside
Leaving a city is a long background plus one short event, and English tells the two parts with different tenses
Why large cities are bad places to live

items: The text says leaving a city is usually one single decision.
It says it almost never is: there is a long background and then one very short event.
The small ordinary things are not reasons to leave on their own.
Traffic, space, bad sleep — not one of them is a reason. Together, over years, they are the reason.
According to the text, the sharp event is told with was and were plus -ing.
The opposite. The short event takes the plain past; the long background takes was and were plus -ing.
Using the wrong tense makes the story impossible to understand.
It says the story still makes sense. What it loses is its shape.
The tenses are what let the listener hear when the decision was made.
If everything sounds equally important, the moment of the decision disappears.

items.situation: Somebody asks how you ended up living where you live. Start with the background, not with the fact.
tips: I was living in Sao Paulo and spending three hours a day in traffic.
Start with was or were plus -ing: it tells the listener this part lasted.

items.situation: The same person asks what finally made you decide. Give the short event.
tips: One Tuesday I was sitting in gridlock and I just snapped.
Plain past for the event: it happened once and it was over.

items.situation: Say what was going on around you while you were making up your mind.
tips: While I was mulling it over, my husband found the house.
while plus was or were -ing, then the plain past for what happened.

items.situation: Somebody asks whether it was a sudden decision. Say it was not.
tips: It was not on a whim. I mulled it over for two years.
on a whim is the exact opposite of what you want to say here.

items.situation: Say that somebody tried to stop you, and what they claimed.
tips: Two people tried to talk me out of it. They said I was being restless.
was being plus adjective = behaving that way at that time, not permanently.

items.situation: Say the moment you finally acted, in one sentence.
tips: In March I packed up the apartment and took the plunge.
Two plain past verbs in a row: that is what a decision sounds like.

answerkey.title: Reveal the whole narrative key
key: The background, and how long it lasted: I was living / I was spending / I was telling everybody I was fine
The short event that ended it: the bus did not come / I snapped / I said it out loud
The two joined: I was sitting in traffic WHEN I made the decision
The other order: WHILE I was mulling it over, my husband found the house
when + plain past · while + was or were -ing. Almost always.
State verbs stay simple: I knew, I understood, I wanted — never I was knowing
was being + adjective = behaving that way then: They said I was being restless
The sentence that ends every version of this story: It was not a whim.
